title: Game 12: Hans vs Magnus
notes: Game 12 of 12 in the experiment, from the Queen's Gambit Declined. Magnus (the learner) reads his notebook and similar past mistakes before every move; Hans (the control) has neither.

This is the classical Queen's Gambit Declined; I want to complete development while keeping the central tension, so e3 supports d4 and opens the f1-bishop's diagonal. Nxd5 loses a piece to Nxd5 and cxd5 releases the tension too early, so the solid e3 is best.

This is the standard Queen's Gambit Declined Classical setup, and my notebook says to develop and castle before any central break, so I tuck the king away with ...O-O. I checked White's replies: Bxf6 Bxf6 is harmless, cxd5 exd5 is normal, and nothing hits my loose pieces since Be7 is defended by queen and rook after castling.

This is a standard Queen's Gambit Declined structure, so I want to complete development naturally rather than grab on d5 (6.Nxd5 exd5 7.cxd5 Nxd5 just frees Black's game). Nf3 develops the last kingside piece, supports d4 and e5 ideas, and keeps the option of Bd3/Rc1 with a comfortable space edge.

I want a solid developing move rather than a pawn push in front of my king, so I checked that 6...Nbd7 leaves nothing loose: 7.cxd5 exd5 is fine, and 7.Bxf6 Nxf6 just trades off my well-defended knight. This finishes my minor-piece development in the Queen's Gambit Declined and keeps ...c6/...dxc4 or ...Ne4 ideas available.

This is the Classical Queen's Gambit Declined with Nbd7; the standard plan is to complete development and build pressure on the c-file before committing the light-squared bishop. The tactical try 7.Nxd5 exd5 8.cxd5 Nxd5 just loses a knight for a pawn, so I'll develop naturally with Rc1, keeping options of Bd3 or cxd5 next.

This is the main-line Queen's Gambit Declined after 7.Rc1, and the standard solid continuation is 7...c6, supporting d5 and preparing the Capablanca freeing maneuver with ...dxc4 and ...Nd5 later; I checked White's captures (Bxf6 Nxf6, cxd5 exd5) and nothing wins material. Premature breaks like ...e5 or ...c5 or releasing the tension with ...dxc4 right now would just give White the better structure and tempo.

This is the classical QGD with Rc1 already in; the natural developing move is Bd3, completing development and preparing castling while keeping pressure. Tactics like Nxd5 fail (cxd5 just wins a piece), and after 8.Bd3 dxc4 9.Bxc4 I get a comfortable isolated-pawn-free setup with a strong center.

I'm fully developed and castled, so the standard Capablanca freeing manoeuvre applies: 8...dxc4 9.Bxc4 Nd5 trades off a pair of pieces and relieves the cramp, and I checked that the Greek-gift try 9.Bxh7+ Kxh7 10.Ng5+ Kg6 11.h4 f5 holds since my knights cover the e4/f6 squares. Nothing of mine is loose after the capture and the c4 pawn cannot be held by White's pieces otherwise.

Black has just grabbed the c4 pawn, so I simply recapture to restore material and keep my strong bishop on the b3-g8 diagonal with ideal development. The Bxh7+ sacrifice doesn't work yet since Black's knight on d7 and bishop on e7 cover g5/h4 ideas, so the sound recapture is best.

With my bishop on c4 attacked I gain a tempo with the standard Semi-Slav 9...b5, kicking it and preparing ...a6 and the ...c5 break once everything is developed. I checked the tactics: 10.Bxb5 cxb5 11.Nxb5 and 10.Nxb5 cxb5 11.Bxb5 both give White only two pawns for a knight, 10.Bxf6 just trades off, and 10.d5 cxd5 11.Nxd5 Nxd5 12.Bxd5 exd5 leaves me a piece up for a pawn.

Black's 9...b5 hits my bishop, so I need to retreat it; Bd3 keeps the strong diagonal toward h7 and prepares to castle, whereas Bb3 would be awkward after a later b4 and Be2 is passive. After Bd3 b4 I can simply play Ne4, trading into a comfortable position with pressure on the kingside.

My b5 pawn is the only loose point and White's Rc1/Nc3 eye the c-file, so I solidify with 10...a6, keeping the pawn chain intact and preparing the ...c5 break once ...Bb7 is in; I checked that 11.Bxb5 axb5 12.Nxb5 cxb5 just loses a piece for White and 11.Bxf6 Nxf6 changes nothing. Immediate 10...c5 11.dxc5 Nxc5 leaves b5 hanging to Nxb5, and 10...b4 11.Na4 leaves that pawn loose, so the quiet consolidating move is best.

I checked the Greek-gift 11.Bxh7+ Kxh7 12.Ng5+, but Black's extra defenders (Nf6, Be7, Nd7) hold everything — after 12...Kg8 13.Nxe6 fxe6 I'd just be down a bishop and knight for two pawns. So I'll complete development safely with castling, keeping my pleasant space edge and the option of a4 or e4 next.

The thematic Meran-style break 11...c5 is the main line here, freeing my game before White consolidates with e4 or a4; I checked that dxc5 is answered by ...Nxc5 (c5 is defended twice by Nd7 and Be7) and that the Greek gift 12.Bxh7+ Kxh7 13.Ng5+ simply fails to 13...Bxg5 14.Bxg5 Qxg5, since the queen on d1 never covers g5. The d4-d5 push is also harmless after ...exd5 recapturing with the pawn rather than the knight, keeping the c8-h3 diagonal and b5 protected.

Black's queenside is still undeveloped (Bc8, Ra8 loose), so I want to open the center immediately with the thematic 12.d5. After 12...exd5 13.Bxf6 Nxf6 14.Nxd5 Nxd5 15.Qxd5 my queen hits both a8 and the weak c5 pawn (only defended once, attacked by Q and Rc1), winning a pawn; other recaptures let me regain material with Nxd5 and pressure on the c-file.

I checked the capture chain: 12...Nxd5 13.Nxd5 exd5 is a clean knight-for-knight trade (my e6 pawn is the only defender, so the recapture is forced and equal), after which 14.Bxe7 Qxe7 leaves c5 guarded by Nd7 against Rxc5, and the Bxb5/Bxh7+ sacrifices only give White two pawns for a bishop. I preferred this to 12...exd5, where 13.Bxf6 and Nxd5 with the Bxh7+ resource strips my centre, since capturing with the knight keeps a solid pawn pair on c5/d5 and my king intact.

I'm a pawn down after 12...Nxd5, so I need the cleanest way to generate pressure: 13.Nxd5 forces 13...exd5 (13...Bxg5 14.Nxg5 exd5 15.Qxd5 regains everything with threats on f7/a8), leaving Black with hanging c5/d5 pawns and a passive bishop on c8. Then Bxe7, Qc2 and Rfd1 give me real play against d5 and h7, while sacrifices like Bxh7+ just lose a piece for pawns.

White's Nd5 is attacking my Be7 and is only attackable by my e6-pawn, so I checked every alternative: 13...Bxg5 14.Ne7+! forks king and Bc8, and 13...Bd6/Nf6/Ne5/Qa5 all let White save the knight (Nxe7+ or Nf4) leaving him a minor piece up for a pawn. Therefore 13...exd5 is the only recapture that restores material; after 14.Bxe7 Qxe7 15.Bxh7+ Kxh7 16.Qd3+ Kg8 17.Qxd5 I am a pawn down but get ...Nb6/...Bb7 with active play, which beats losing a piece.

Black is threatening ...Bxg5, since after Nxg5 the queen recaptures via d8-e7-f6-g5, so I must handle that while hitting the loose d5 pawn (Nd7 blocks the queen's defence). Be4 does both: it attacks d5, discourages ...c4 and ...f5 (Bxd5+ picking up a8), and after 14...Bxg5 15.Nxg5 Qxg5 16.Bxd5 I regain material by hitting a8, while 14...Nf6 15.Bxf6 Bxf6 16.Rxc5 wins the pawn back.

White's 14.Be4 attacks my d5 pawn, but e4 is defended by nothing — the knight on f3, the queen on d1 and both rooks don't cover that square — so the pawn capture simply wins a bishop. I checked the follow-ups: 15.Bxe7 Qxe7, 15.Qxd7 Bxd7 and 15.Qd5 Nb6/Bxg5 all leave me a clean piece ahead (my e4 pawn even hits the f3 knight), and White has no checks at all.

I'm down a piece after the exchanges, and my Bg5 is only "defended" by Nf3 — illusory, since after Be7xg5, Nxg5 runs into Qd8xg5 along the vacated diagonal; meanwhile the e4 pawn hits my knight. So I must resolve both problems at once by trading bishops first: Bxe7 Qxe7 and then Nd2, which saves the knight and immediately attacks the loose e4 pawn (and hits c4/b3 ideas against b5/c5). Taking with 15...exf3 instead fails to 16.Bxd8 winning the queen.

Counting material, I'm already up a minor piece and a pawn, so I simply recapture the bishop with 15...Qxe7, which also keeps c5 doubly guarded (Nd7 and the queen) and leaves White's f3 knight hanging to my e4 pawn. I checked White's replies: Rxc5 Nxc5, Qd5 exf3 (and ...Bb7 traps the queen if Qxa8), and there are no checks against my king.

My knight on f3 is attacked by the e4 pawn and must move; Nd4 and Ne5 just drop material (cxd4 or Nxe5 with no recapture), and Ng5/Nh4 get chased awkwardly. Nd2 keeps everything defended, hits the loose e4 pawn, and heads for b3/c4 to pressure Black's weak queenside pawns.

I'm up a bishop and a pawn, so I just need to consolidate: my e4 pawn is attacked by Nd2 and currently undefended, so 16...Bb7 both develops my last piece and guards e4 along the long diagonal. I checked White's tries: 17.Nxe4 Bxe4 just loses a piece, and 17.Qf3 hits e4 and b7 but e4 is covered by the bishop and b7 by Ra8, so nothing hangs.

Nxe4 and Rxc5 both lose material (Bxe4 with no recapture, and Qxc5 from e7), so I need to build pressure instead. Qc2 adds a second attacker to the loose e4 pawn (threatening Nxe4 Bxe4 Qxe4) while doubling on the c-file against the weak c5 pawn, and my queen is completely safe there.

I'm up a bishop and a pawn, and White's 17.Qc2 adds a second attacker to my e4 pawn (Qc2 and Nd2) which only Bb7 defends. Nf6 develops the knight and gives e4 a second defender, so 18.Nxe4 Nxe4 19.Qxe4 Bxe4 just loses White's queen, and if White plays f3 I keep a winning material edge anyway.

I'm material down (a bishop for a pawn after the earlier mess), so I want to simplify and grab compensation; the c5 pawn is defended only by the queen on e7. 18.Qxc5 Qxc5 19.Rxc5 wins a pawn and trades queens, whereas capturing on e4 first fails tactically (18.Nxe4 Nxe4 19.Qxe4 Bxe4 drops my queen, and 19.f3 Nxf2 wrecks my king cover).

I'm up a full bishop (B+N vs N with equal pawns), so the simplest path is to liquidate: Qxc5 Rxc5 is a clean one-for-one queen trade (c5 is covered by the Rc1, nothing more), leaving me a piece ahead in a simple endgame. I checked the follow-up captures: my e4 pawn is attacked by Nd2 but guarded twice by Bb7 and Nf6, and b5 after Rxc5 is held by the a6 pawn, so no counter-tactics exist.
Black recaptured on c5 with the queen, but c5 is covered by my rook on c1 — the b5 pawn can't capture backwards and no knight or bishop guards the square. Rxc5 simply wins the queen for a rook.

I'm a full bishop up (B+N vs N), so simplification is my friend — I offer the rook trade with Rfc8, and after 20.Rxc8+ Rxc8 nothing is loose: e4 is guarded by Bb7, a6 by Bb7, f7 by my king, so Nxe4 just loses the knight. Rxb5 is impossible because axb5 wins the rook, and if White declines with Rc7 I simply take it.

I'm down a minor piece, so I need activity and material back: Rxb5 grabs a pawn and simultaneously attacks the b7 bishop along the open b-file. If Black ignores it with Rc2 hitting my knight, then Rxb7 Rxd2 leaves me with equal rooks and a pawn plus, and otherwise Bc6 just lets me retreat a pawn up.

My bishop on b7 is hanging to Rb5, so I must address it; Bc6 both saves the bishop on a square no White piece attacks and counterattacks the rook, winning a tempo. I checked White's replies: Nxe4 loses to Bxb5, and any rook retreat like Rb6 is met by ...Rc6 or ...Bd5 since c6 is guarded by my rook, so I keep my extra piece.

My rook on b5 is attacked by the bishop on c6, so I must move it, and Nxe4 fails to Nxe4 followed by Bxb5. Rb4 retreats safely while attacking the loose e4 pawn, which I can hit again with the knight and rooks; if Black tries Nd5 forking b4 and e3, I simply take with Rxe4 since Nxe3 then loses the knight to fxe3.

White's Rb4 is undefended and the b5-f1 diagonal is wide open, so Bb5 hits both rooks at once — the bishop is defended by a6, so Rxb5 axb5 loses a rook for a bishop, and any rook retreat (Rb3, a4, Rc4, Rxe4) allows ...Bxf1 Kxf1 winning rook for bishop. I checked White's counters: no checks exist, 22.Nxe4 Nxe4 23.Rxe4 Bxf1 24.Kxf1 leaves me a whole rook up, and 22.Nc4 Bxc4 23.Rxc4 Rxc4 likewise wins material.

My rook on f1 is attacked by the bishop on b5, and since it's only defended by the king, any capture there trades bishop for rook in Black's favour — so 22.Rxe4 Bxf1 or 22.Nxe4 Nxe4 23.Rxe4 Bxf1 both cost me material. Instead I step the rook off the diagonal to e1, where it shields e3 and adds a second attacker to the loose e4 pawn (together with Nd2), so I win that pawn back next move.

I'm up a bishop for a pawn, and my only loose unit is the e4 pawn, which Nd2 and Rb4 both hit while only Nf6 guards it. Bc6 adds a second defender from a safe square (nothing attacks c6), and if White starts the exchange 23.Nxe4 Nxe4 24.Rxe4 Bxe4 25.Rxe4 I end up with two rooks against one, so I keep both the extra piece and the extra pawn without offering any trade.

I'm down a bishop for a pawn, so I need activity rather than exchanges; the triple attack on e4 (Nxe4/Rxe4) doesn't work because the recaptures cost me a rook for a bishop. Instead 23.Nc4 improves my worst piece with the strong follow-up Nd6, hitting the c8 rook, f7 and e4, while also covering e3 so ...Nd5 ideas are harmless.

I'm up a bishop for a pawn, so I need to answer the Nc4 threats (Nd6 hitting c8/e4, Na5/Ne5 hitting my loose bishop) while keeping things simple. I checked Bd5 and found 24.Nb6! (defended by Rb4) forking both rooks and the bishop, so I rejected it; instead Nd5 is untouchable, hits Rb4 and covers b6/e3, and every reply loses material — 24.Ne5/Nd6/Rb6 all run into Nxb4 or Nxb6 with favourable trades, and 24.Rb5/Rb7 drop to Bxb5/Bxb7.

My rook on b4 is attacked by the knight on d5, and most rook moves run into tactics (Rb5/Ra4 drop to Bxb5/Bxa4, Rb7 to Bxb7, Rb6 to Nxb6, Rb8 to Rxb8), while Nd6 loses material after Nxb4 Nxc8 Rxc8. Rb3 keeps the rook active, guards b2, and keeps my knight on c4 so I can later hit the loose e4 pawn with Nd2; Black's tries like Bb5 run into Nd6 forking c8 and b5, and Nxe3 just loses a piece to fxe3.

I'm up a bishop for a pawn, so my priority is safety and consolidation rather than grabbing: I checked that 24...Nb6 and 24...Bb5 run into Nxb6 (my knight there is undefended) and the Nd6 fork hitting b5, while my loose e4 pawn is the only real target. 24...Nf6 defends e4, keeps every piece protected (Bc6 by Rc8, a6 by Ra8, f7 by the king), and leaves White no check, capture or fork — after Nd6 I simply play Rd8 and kick the knight, then trade rooks and convert the extra piece.

review.label: blunder
review.refutation: 25. Nb6 Bd7 26. Nxa8 Rxa8 27. Rc1 g6

moves.thought: Black's rooks on a8 and c8 only defend each other, so 25.Nb6 forks them while being protected by my rook on b3 — any defence still allows Nxc8 or Nxa8, winning rook for knight and erasing Black's extra piece. Even the trickiest reply 25...Bd5 (hitting my rook) lets me answer Rb4 and still collect a rook with the knight.

White's Nb6 forks my rooks on a8 and c8, and simply defending a rook doesn't help since knight-takes-rook still wins the exchange, so I need a counterattack of equal value: 25...Bd5 hits the undefended Rb3 while being safely defended by Nf6. If 26.Nxa8 Bxb3 27.axb3 Rxa8 the trades are even and I keep my extra piece; 26.Nxd5 Nxd5 dissolves the fork entirely, and only an awkward rook retreat like 26.Rd3 keeps White's threat alive.

My knight on b6 forks both rooks, but Black's bishop on d5 hits my rook on b3, so I must relocate it while keeping the fork alive — Rb4 is safe from everything, keeps the fork, defends the knight on b6, and hits the e4 pawn. After the likely 26...Rcb8 I get 27.Nxd5 Nxd5 28.Rxb8+ Rxb8 29.Rxe4, recovering a pawn; and if Black plays anything other than a rook to b8 (e.g. Bc6 or Nd7) I simply win a rook for the knight or pick off the bishop.

My bishop on d5 is attacked by Nb6 and undefended, so it must move; Bxa2 and Bc4 lose material (Nxc8/Rxc4 tricks), so I retreat to b7 where the bishop is safe and simultaneously defends both a8 and c8 against the knight fork and covers c6. White can only grab the e4 pawn with Rxe4, after which I'm still a clean piece up and can play ...Rc6 (protected by the bishop) to harass the trapped-looking knight on b6.

review.label: blunder
review.refutation: 27. Nxa8 Bxa8 28. Rb6 Nd5 29. Rxa6 Nb4

moves.thought: My knight on b6 is untouchable but both black rooks are on the eighth rank, so I can simply trade it for a rook — Nxa8 Rxa8 leaves me a rook for a knight up, which restores full material equality (2R+6P vs R+B+N+5P). I prefer taking on a8 so Black's remaining rook is left passive guarding a6 rather than active on the c-file.

The knight on a8 is trapped and must be taken or it escapes via b6 with me a rook down, and both recaptures give the same material (B+N vs R with pawns level), so I choose the one that keeps my rook active: Bxa8 leaves the rook on the open c-file ready to invade on c2 while the bishop still guards my e4 pawn (so Rxe4 loses a rook). I noted that ...Rc1 later would simply drop a rook to Rxe1xc1, so my plan is Rc2 hitting b2/f2, happily trading one pair of rooks since two pieces for a rook favours me.

Black's a6 pawn is loose and the bishop on a8 sits on the same file, so Ra4 both attacks a6 and sets up a lethal a-file skewer — lines like 28...Rb8 29.Rxa6 Rxb2 30.Rxa8+ Ne8 31.Rxe8+ end in mate, and 28...Nd5 29.Rxa6 hits the bishop too. Black's only real defence is the passive 28...Rc6, after which I double with Rea1 and win the pawn anyway.

Ra4 is hitting my undefended a6 pawn, and my a8 bishop is loose on the a-file, so anything like Rc2 runs into Rxa6 hitting the bishop and Rxa8. Bb7 solves both problems at once: it guards a6, steps off the a-file, and activates the bishop, and I checked White has no capture or check against it (Rb4 is answered by Bd5/Bc6).

Both captures lose material — e4 is defended by both the knight and the bishop, and a6 is covered by the bishop on b7, so Rxe4 and Rxa6 just drop a rook. Instead I undermine the advanced e4 pawn with f3, when exf3 gxf3 leaves me a clean extra pawn with a solid center, and Nd5 fails to fxe4 Nxe3 Rxe3.

My e4 pawn is defended twice (Bb7 along a8–h1 and Nf6), so f3 is no real threat, and Rc3 would lose to bxc3 while Nd5 would self-block the bishop's defence of e4. The active Rc2 runs into 30.Rd1 with Rd8+ ideas against my untouched f7-g7-h7 back rank (…Rxb2 31.Rd8+ even gets mated), so per my rule I create luft first with h6 and keep all the tension, intending Rc2 next.

review.label: mistake
review.refutation: 30. Rf1 Rc2 31. Rf2 Rc7 32. h3 g6

moves.thought: Black's e4 pawn is defended twice (Bb7 and Nf6), so Rxe4 just loses a rook for a knight and a pawn; instead fxe4 forces Black to recapture with the knight and leaves me a pawn up (5 vs 4) with two rooks against bishop and knight, where fewer pawns favors my rooks. Rxa6 fails too since the bishop on b7 covers a6.

I noticed that the e4 pawn is attacked twice (Bb7, Nf6) but defended only once, since White's Re1 is blocked by its own e3 pawn — so I simply win a pawn. I prefer Nxe4 over Bxe4 because the knight on e4 stays defended by the bishop while the bishop on b7 keeps guarding a6 (after Bxe4, Rxa6 grabs it back), and if Rxe4 then Bxe4 leaves me a whole rook for the knight; next I plan Rc2 hitting b2 and g2.

review.label: mistake
review.refutation: 31. Rb4 Rc7 32. h3 Bd5 33. Rd4 Nf6

moves.thought: Rxe4 and Rxa6 both just lose a rook to the bishop's recapture, and Rc1 loses a rook outright to Rxc1+ since my a4-rook can't cover c1. Rb4 instead hits the undefended bishop on b7 and sidesteps the Nc3 fork ideas against a4/e2, keeping my rook active with pressure on b7 and a6.

Checking White's captures I saw that 31.Rb4 double-attacked my knight on e4 (held by Bb7) and, crucially, the loose bishop on b7 down the open b-file, so Rxb7 was threatened. 31...Nc5 solves everything with one move: the knight steps off the attacked square, defends b7 and a6, and stays untouchable by either rook, keeping my full extra piece without any trade.

review.label: blunder
review.refutation: 32. Rc1 Bd5 33. Rd4 Be6 34. b4 Nb7

moves.thought: Rxb7 just loses a rook for a bishop, and a4/e4/Rb3/Rc4 all drop material to the active knight on c5 (Nxa4, Nxe4, Nxb3, Rxc4). Rd4 is a safe central square the knight and bishop cannot touch, it seizes the d-file so I can double with Re1-d1 and invade on d7/d8, and it keeps my two rooks coordinated against the weak a6 pawn.

I checked every capture first: Rd8 and Bd5 just drop a piece to Rxd8+/Rxd5, and Nb3/Na4/Nd3 fall to axb3/Rxa4/Rxd3, while Bxg2 loses to Kxg2. Ne6 is defended by f7, hits the loose rook on d4 with tempo, and after 33.Rd6 or Rd7 I answer Rc6/Rc7 to force a rook trade into a comfortable bishop-and-knight-versus-rook ending, with my back rank still covered by Rc8.

I'm two rooks against rook, bishop and knight with an extra pawn, so I want activity and must avoid trading a rook off. 33.Rd7 seizes the seventh rank, hits f7, and if Black blocks with ...Rd8 I get 34.Ra7 hitting the loose bishop and a6; ...Rc2 fails to 34.Rxf7, and ...Bc6 leaves a6 hanging to Ra7.

My bishop on b7 is attacked by Rd7, and since I'm the side with bishop+knight against two rooks, every rook-for-rook trade helps me — so 33...Rc7 both defends the bishop and offers the trade, with the rook protected by Ne6. After 34.Rxc7 Nxc7 I have B+N+4 pawns against R+5 pawns, roughly balanced, and if White declines with 34.Rd8+ Kh7 I keep the defence intact.

review.label: mistake
review.refutation: 34. Red1 Rxd7 35. Rxd7 Bc6 36. Ra7 Bb5

moves.thought: My d7 rook is attacked and retreating lets Black's rook invade (Rc2) or force the exchange anyway on better terms (Rc6 and Bxc6), while Re7 and Rxf7 just drop a rook to Rxe7/Rxf7. Trading now removes Black's only active piece and leaves his knight and bishop passive, with my rook plus extra queenside pawn giving good practical chances to hold and push a4/b4.

White's rook took on c7 and I must simply recapture — Nxc7 wins back the rook, leaving me bishop and knight against a single rook with pawns level (5 v 4 in my favour). No white check or capture follows: 35.Re8+ Kh7 or 35.Re7 Nd5 is fine, so I take the rook as my notebook says.

Material is roughly balanced (rook and five pawns against two pieces and four pawns), so I want activity: the plan is Rd1 followed by Rd7 hitting f7 and b7. Playing e4 first takes the d5 square away from the knight so it can't blockade the open file, and it starts rolling my pawns.

Bxe4 loses a piece to Rxe4 since the rook on e1 guards it, so instead I put the bishop on d5 where no pawn can ever chase it: it attacks the passed e4 pawn, controls the e6 blockading square in front of it, and gets my bishop off the diagonal that White's e-pawn had shut down. With bishop and knight against rook I need my pieces coordinated around that passer, and the knight can follow to e6/d4 next.

review.label: blunder
review.refutation: 36. exd5 Kf8 37. Re4 Nxd5 38. Ra4 Nc7

moves.thought: Black's bishop just stepped onto d5 where my e4 pawn can simply take it; the knight on c7 recaptures, so I trade a pawn for a whole bishop. That leaves rook and four pawns against knight and four pawns, a winning material edge with no tactics against my rook on e1.

White's exd5 left the d5 pawn completely undefended — no rook or king covers it — so Nxd5 recaptures the dangerous passer for free and leaves me only a rook-for-knight down with four pawns each. After Nxd5 the only forcing try is Re8+ Kh7, and then any rook attack on my knight (Re5) is met by a simple retreat, so nothing is lost.

I'm a full rook for knight ahead with equal pawns, and my a2/b2 duo gives a 2-v-1 queenside majority, so the cleanest winning plan is to advance it: b4 then b5 to create a passed pawn while my rook stays ready to swing to the b-file. Black's knight can't blockade effectively, and nothing on b4 is attackable — the alternative Re5 hitting the knight just lets it hop away without progress.

White's b4 pawn is simply free — Nxb4 wins it and leaves White's a2 pawn permanently blocked by my a6, giving me knight + 4 pawns against rook + 3 with only one effective pawn island for him. I checked the activity tricks: Re8+ Kh7 Re7 is met by Kg6 defending f7 and g7, and any Ra7/Re6 raid on a6 fails because my knight on b4 guards a6.

My a2 pawn is attacked by the knight on b4, so I push it to a4 where the knight can't reach it, keeping my extra material and fixing Black's a6 pawn as a permanent target for my rook (Re6/Rb6 ideas). Immediately playing Re4 would allow 38...Nxa2 39.Ra4 Nc3 and only an equal pawn trade, whereas a4 keeps three pawns plus a future passer if I win a6.

White's a-pawn is his only potential passer, so I stop it permanently with ...a5, after which the a-pawns block each other and the game reduces to my knight and 3 kingside pawns against his rook and 2 — a comfortable holding setup. If 39.Re4 hits my knight, 39...Nc6 both saves it and defends a5, and the knight can shuttle c6/b3 to keep guarding the pawn.

The a-pawns are locked, so I looked for an active rook move, and Re5 hits the undefended a5 pawn along the fifth rank while keeping my rook flexible. If Black plays Nd3 to hit the rook I simply take with Rxa5, and after Nc6 defending, his knight is tied down while I bring my king up.

White's rook on e5 hits my undefended a5 pawn, so I checked which knight move both saves it and gains time: Nc6 defends a5 and simultaneously attacks the rook on e5, so Rxa5 just loses the rook to Nxa5. The knight on c6 is untouchable by anything White has, so White must retreat the rook and I keep knight plus four pawns against rook plus three.

My rook on e5 is attacked by the knight, so I must move it, and Rc5 is ideal: it's immune to the knight, attacks the undefended knight on c6, and simultaneously eyes the a5 pawn. If the knight steps away (e.g. Nd4 or Nb4) it stops guarding a5, so Rxa5 follows and my rook-for-knight edge plus the passed a-pawn should decide the game.

White's Rc5 threatens 41.Rc8+ Kh7 42.Rxc6, winning my undefended knight on a back-rank check, so I must give my king luft; Kh7 does that while keeping the knight on c6 guarding a5 (41.Rxa5? new_lessons: [middlegame] Before any move, list enemy checks, captures and pawn-captures hitting your destination square; never place a piece where a pawn can take it for less value Example: 35...Bd5?? 36.exd5 swapped my extra bishop for a pawn, 51%→8%

[middlegame] When material up, trace every enemy knight two moves ahead for forks (Nc4-b6 hitting a8/c8); kill the entry square or step the attacked rook away, not the bishop Example: 24...Nf6? and 26...Bb7? allowed Nb6xa8; 24...Ba4/26...Rcb8 kept the piece

[endgame] With two minor pieces versus a rook, refuse every piece-for-pawn trade; blockade the passer with the knight, keep the bishop on a pawn-free diagonal, march the king in Example: 35...Ne6 held; 35...Bd5 36.exd5 collapsed to rook versus knight

[endgame] In rook endings, before every rook move ask if an enemy rook can land on your back rank; with king behind untouched f2-g2-h2, play h3/g3 or Kf1 first, or meet an invading rook with Rd1/Rd2 opposition Example: 29.Rd4?? Rc1+ 30.Rd1 Rxd1 mate, 56%→2%

[endgame] When your rook can capture an enemy rook with check, take it; fear of a pawn race never justifies declining a capture with check while material up Example: 28.Rd3+ instead of 28.Rxc7+ threw away 82%→54%

[endgame] With extra material trade one-for-one but never your last extra piece; cut off his king, take the seventh rank, push a passer only with escort Example: Refusing 31.Rd5 dropped 94%→61%; 59...b5 pushed an unescorted pawn

[endgame] Before each endgame move check enemy Kx-captures and stalemate tricks, keep extra pawns connected, and stay inside the square of every enemy passer Example: 66...Qc3+? Kxc3 drew a won queen endgame; 29...dxc4 scattered a6/c4/c6

[middlegame] Before trading a minor piece, play out the recapture: if a pawn recapture opens a file or diagonal toward your king or leaves pawns loose, keep the piece Example: 17...Nc4 18.Bxc4 dxc4 opened the e-file for Re4 and left c4 hanging, 51%→9%

[middlegame] When one of your pieces is attacked, first look for a pawn move that counterattacks or gains tempo, and test whether a check removes the retreat square Example: 25...Nd6? lost to 26.Qg5+ Kh7 27.Qxf6; 25...c5 held

[middlegame] When your rook can invade the enemy second rank hitting loose pawns, prefer that to any equal trade; with exposed kings activity beats simplification Example: Instead of 17...Nc4, 17...Rf2 grabbing h2 and tying White down was winning

[middlegame] Never push pawns in front of your castled king while an enemy bishop or queen eyes those squares; answer a wing storm with a central break Example: 17.g3 invited ...fxg3 and ...Bxh3; 17.dxc6 kept a winning game

[opening] When a bishop pins your knight against king or a loose piece, kick the pinner with a3/h3 or block with Bd2 instead of defending passively with the queen Example: 12.Qd2 let ...Nc5-e4 pile on; 12.a3 questioned Bb4 at once
